No. I am not suggesting that we take it away from the provinces. I am suggesting that, rather than go down into the pocket of the poor man in this country, the government might impose a bit more taxation upon amusements of one kind and another. I am always rather intrigued by these references to the capital gains tax. I

realize that there are arguments against it; but, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that there are many things that I would do, even though I might not like them too much, before I would go down into the pocket of the fellow who today is going through a great deal of misery in an effort to provide for his family.
There was one other matter to which I wished to refer. I should not suggest that I could be out of order, Mr. Chairman; I should not give you any ideas on that score, because when it comes to that, you have plenty of ideas yourself. In the course of the consideration of the sales tax, certain hon. members have asserted that other things could have been done rather than to have increased the sales tax. Some hon. members asserted that the government might have lifted the income tax a little more in order to offset the need of the sales tax. The minister asserted that it would hurt too much if you hit them a little too hard at one time. In 1933 the former minister of finance, Mr. Ilsley, who had frequently attacked the sales tax during those years the Conservatives were in office and were increasing it, said that instead of imposing an iniquitous tax of this kind the government would be justified in taking a man's entire income from him over and above a certain amount. I will not quote his statement because I hardly think that would be in order; but it may be found at page 3495 of Hansard of March 28, 1933. I only pass on the observation, not that I am advocating that a man's entire income be taken away from him; I did it to show the difference between a Liberal who is a member of the government and a Liberal who finds himself on the opposition side of the house.
How does that work out?
Mr. Chairman, if there are to be interjections, I hope they will be loud enough so that I can at least hear them.
What was the total budget at that time?

An hon. member asks what the total budget was. It is not a matter of the total budget; it is the total tax revenue in relation to the national income. It is the relationship between what the government is taking from the pockets of the people and the national income of your country. And if my hon. friend takes the figures in those days and compares them with the figures of today, he will find that the tax hurt proportionately as much at that time.
In conclusion, I am going to re-assert one or two things that I said at the beginning. I dislike the sales tax so intensely that I for
Excise Tax Act
one am opposing this resolution; I am not supporting any 25 per cent increase in the sales tax at this time-that is a favourite government expression. I am not supporting the 10 per cent increase in the excise tax, as applied to a long list of commodities. But let me point out that my principal reason for opposing the resolution as such is first of all the sales tax. I know that as long as the present government occupies office we are going to have to contemplate from time to time rather stiff increases in taxation. I am going to be perfectly fair to them and also say that as long as the international situation is such as it is, we are likely to have that inevitable result. I am not going to take such strong opposition with respect to the other commodities listed here and the taxation increases in relation thereto, but I am taking a very firm position as far as this sales tax is concerned. As far as I personally am concerned, I am opposing this resolution which is proposing to amend the Excise Tax Act.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am sure the parliamentary assistant does not want the resolution to carry before he has had a chance to answer some of the questions put to him the other night. He will recall that the hon. member for Lake Centre put a certain question to him, which I elaborated. It had to do with the effect of the tax changes involved in the Excise Tax Act proposals on the cost of living of what might be called the average Canadian family. I do not think I need to go into detail again in the way in which I set it out before the parliamentary assistant the other night, unless he asks me to do so. Perhaps he can answer that question now.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The hon. member for Lake Centre asked that as well as the table that I put on the record from the dominion bureau of statistics showing the percentage of income in various groups which was subject to sales tax, I should also try to obtain from the dominion bureau of statistics what this increase in sales tax and excise tax actually meant in dollars and cents to families in various income groups. We got in touch with the dominion bureau of statistics and they said it was impossible for them statistically to work out such a thing. They could work out the percentage of income which is subject to tax just by using the analysis they had in 1947-1948 of how families in various income tax groups spent their money on the commodities. The mathematical problem of determining what this two per cent increase in the sales tax, the ten per cent increase in the excise tax and the fifteen per cent increase on electrical appliances means in dollars and cents to the individual

Excise Tax Act
consumer is tied in, as I indicated when I was answering the hon. member, with the problem of mark-up. Unless the mathematical analysis over in the dominion bureau of statistics gives the mark-up in each of the various commodities there is no real base to submit a mathematical figure. For that reason they said it was impossible to do better than they have done by breaking it into percentages.
The hon. member for Lake Centre seemed to think that I had such figures with me. Probably the reason for his supposition was the fact that one of the members of the press gallery had an article in one of the Toronto papers with his calculations of what this would amount to. I have spoken to him. These are his calculations based actually on the break-down which I put on the record, and which he had obtained previously from the dominion bureau of statistics.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I suppose we have to take it that the dominion bureau of statistics is unable to answer that type of question. Frankly that does amaze me. I can understand the bureau not knowing in advance what the additional effect of mark-ups might be, but it does seem to me that it should be able to compute what the increases in the cost of the articles included in the cost of living index will be as a result of the tax itself.
As I understand it, there is nothing mysterious about the way in which this cost of living index figure is arrived at. I understand that when the 1935-39 base of 100 was arrived at, it was ascertained on the basis of what it actually cost in that 1935-39 period to purchase a certain total basket of goods and services, which was taken to be the standard of living of an average Canadian family at that time. I understand that the way in which the cost of living index is adjusted is for the dominion bureau of statistics to find out each month what that same original basket of goods and services costs. The original cost in the base period was $1,453 a year. Since the cost of living index now stands at something over 180-we will know the exact figure in a day or two- it means that that basket of goods and services is already well up over $2,000. My colleague, the hon. member for Melfort, put the exact figure on the record yesterday.
Well, now, the dominion bureau of statistics is ascertaining information of this kind every day. They put out releases of one kind and another literally every day, and give a very good service in the statistical field. It seems to me that all they have to do to answer the kind of question that I put to

the parliamentary assistant is to go over the goods and services that are included in the original basket, and ascertain how much was added to their price on April 10 by the taxes that were imposed by the minister that night.
As I pointed out when I spoke on this question the other evening, every time the cost of the goods and services in that original basket goes up by $14.53 it means an increase in the cost of living index by one point. Hence I felt it was a perfectly proper question for us to ask as to how many dollars and cents the average Canadian family will have to pay additional on the necessities of life by virtue of the taxes that have been imposed. If the dominion bureau of statistics did the job they would of course do it in relation just to that same original quantity of goods and services. Many Canadian families have rightly a little higher standard of living than was suggested by that 1935-39 basket of goods and services; therefore, to many people the additional cost will be even more than would be the additional cost on that original basket.
I am sure that it is a minimum guess that we make when we suggest that the sales tax and the other taxes in this resolution are going to result in an increase of $40 or $50 in the necessary expenditures of the average Canadian family per year. I may be away out, Mr. Chairman, but if I am, I am away out on the conservative side. It may be twice that amount. But if it means an increase of around $45 in the year, the result will be a rise in the cost of living index of three points.
We were given to understand that this budget was going to deal with the problem of inflation. That was one of the arguments against our starting a certain other debate, which I shall not discuss now. But this is the way, as it strikes some of us, that the budget deals with inflation; it aggravates the problem. We have before us proposals for tax increases on commodities which cannot fail to have the effect of boosting to a higher point the cost of living index. People from coast to coast were shocked with the 4-5 increase on the last occasion the figure was given. We will be receiving another figure in a day or two which will push the figure up from 179-7 to 182 or 183; and in the course of a few months we will have the effects of this budget pushing it up to 185 or 186. The people of Canada will wonder just where this is going to end.
I appreciate that the parliamentary assistant has been in touch with the dominion bureau of statistics, has sought to get the information and has been unsuccessful. But I notice he is discussing the matter-

or discussing something, at any rate-with his officials, while I am talking. I would be glad to have his comments on what I have been asking. Does it not seem to be a reasonable conclusion tor us to draw on this side of the house that the effect of this eight-point resolution we are now asked to vote upon is likely to be an increase in the cost of living index of two, three or more points?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not see
how I can answer more fully than I have done. I have mentioned the factors the dominion bureau of statistics pointed out. The hon. member has said that it should be easy for the dominion bureau of statistics to price today the price of this basket. That is true. They actually have not done it as yet for the month of April, but they will do it.
However, apparently the hon. member intends to go ahead on the assumption that every increase since April 10 is consequent upon the tax increase, and not consequent upon an increased cost of material and an increased cost of labour. That is the problem the bureau of statistics has to contend with -and it is a bureau of statistics, not a guessing bureau.
The second point, so far as the effect upon spending is concerned, is that there is a change in buying methods which the housewife will use, when prices go up. If the price of a frock is increased, she will be content to keep within her budget and to buy a cheaper frock.
I think the figures the hon. member has been quoting are obviously out, when it is remembered that it is the sales tax on commodities which hits the lower income group, rather than the excise tax on luxuries or semiluxuries. If, as he says, the two per cent increase will cost $45, that means that the whole 10 per cent will cost $225, so that the person paying this $225 tax must be buying $2,250 of commodities subject to sales tax, and no low income family does this. So that the hon. member's increase by reason of sales tax is far out of line.
But the dominion bureau of statistics is not in the guessing business. They deal with facts, the cost of these things. When the April cost of living figure comes down the change may or may not be due-whatever changes there are-to the increase in tax. But there will still be other factors which have increased the cost, such as increased labour costs and increased material costs.
I have done my best to obtain these figures from the bureau. They say the only thing they can give us is statistics based upon
Excise Tax Act
actual facts. That is what they have given, and the table I inserted earlier in Hansard gave that information.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I appreciate the table the
parliamentary assistant put on Hansard. I have looked into it, but he will realize it does not deal with the matter we have raised at this time.
I would point out to the parliamentary assistant that the sales tax increase is not the only tax included in the resolution now before us. The eight-paragraph resolution now before us includes the tax on refrigerators, electric stoves, washing machines and the like. I would remind him also that it was he, himself, who said that one of the difficulties of computation would be because these taxes may involve additional markups. So when he looks at my $45 figure he will have to consider not just the effect of the tax itself, but the effect of the tax plus the mark-ups made on it.
I was interested in one of the comments made just now by the parliamentary assistant to the effect that people's buying habits change. He spoke particularly of the housewife. He said that when a housewife goes into a store and finds prices have got out of line she will buy something else, because she cannot afford to buy the article that has gone up to the increased price.
That change in buying habits is not reflected in the cost of living index. The cost of living index is not changed because of change in people's buying habits, whether they raise or lower their standard of living. The parliamentary assistant has said that, so far as the cost of living is concerned, the bureau of statistics does not guess; it gets the actual prices.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
You are talking about how
much extra a person was going to pay. Let us separate the two.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I was talking about the
effect of the resolution now before us on the cost of living index. We are getting two or three points mixed up. The point I was discussing just now was that the effect of the rise in the cost of living index has changed the habits of many people. Indeed it has; it has lowered their standards.
I suppose in the present instance the people of Canada have no alternative but to wait until bitter experience has shown just what the effect of these proposals is on the cost of living. For my part I cannot see that this section of the budget has grappled with the problem of inflation or the cost of living in any way, except to make it worse.

The house in committee on Bill No. 177, to incorporate the Mercantile and General Reinsurance Company of Canada Limited- Mr. Cavers-Mr. Dion in the chair.
Sections 1 and 2 agreed to.
On section 3-Capital stock.

Mr. Chairman, under
this section it is provided that the capital stock of the company shall be $1 million. Would the sponsor explain to me what denominations the shares are to be? Are they to be $100, $500, or what? I understand that the company is to operate in all ten provinces, and I presume the idea would be to have the capital stock distributed as widely as possible among the people of the various provinces. One of my colleagues has suggested to me ten shares of $100,000 each. That is the very reason I should like to say a word on this matter. I understand it is more or less a trend of modern financing- and I know very little about financing-particularly with such companies as this one, to have the capital stock distributed as widely as possible in small denominations in order that the people of the whole dominion will be able to share therein. I presume one reason would be to gain the good will of the people of all the provinces.
Certainly in a company such as this one I would think it would be to their advantage to have the stock issued in small denominations instead of $100,000 shares so the people throughout Canada can purchase the shares. I should like the sponsor to explain to me how it is intended to dispose of the shares. Surely it is not to be, as one of my colleagues has suggested, ten shares of $100,000 each. Possibly it is $50 shares. Would the sponsor explain that point?

Mr. Chairman, I am informed the shares are to sell at a par value of $10 each, and on the matter of the subscription of shares the company must have $250,000 of capital stock subscribed before undertaking any business.

The answer is partly
what I wanted. I was very careful not to mention the figure of $250,000 as that is in the next section, and I was afraid I might be called to order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is section 7.

No, I am speaking on
clause 3.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes.

I am afraid the sponsor was out of order in referring to the next section. I was being very careful not to be out of order, not to transgress by saying anything about section 4. I understand his explanation.

Section agreed to.
Sections 4 to 8 inclusive agreed to.
Preamble agreed to.
On the title.

Before the title carries, if I am in order I want to bring something to the attention of the house. The title of the bill is "An act to incorporate the Mercantile and General Reinsurance Company of Canada Limited." We have no objection to that but I think the government should do something about making certain that companies using the words "Canada limited" are companies that have a federal charter, because that has caused a great deal of misunderstanding among a number of people in my constituency. I refer to the Home Assurance Company of Canada Limited which went into liquidation in 1948. A large number of people in my constituency purchased shares in that company on the understanding that it was a federal company because the words "Canada Limited" were in the title. They thought they were protected by the particular scrutiny of the federal superintendent of insurance, and so on.
These people purchased these shares years ago. There are older people in my riding, just about ready to draw the old age pension, having very few material assets in this life except hope, who bought these shares, a considerable number of which were paid for and some were not paid for. Throughout the years they have had favourable balance sheets indicating that the company was in a wonderful position, and then suddenly it went bankrupt. These people had been under the impression all the time that they were protected by a federal charter. The liquidator of the company is now attempting to collect the balance of the amount payable on certain shares from people over 70 years of age with very little but their homes as assets.

I wish to point that out because I believe that the words "Canada Limited" should not be awarded to any company unless it has a federal charter. I could deal at some length with this matter but I do not want to delay the passage of the bill. I want to bring the matter to the attention of the house because I think it is a point that is worth considering. It involves considerable hardship for a number of very worthy citizens whom I represent who were deluded into investing in what they thought was a company with a federal charter with all the greater security behind that, and who later found that they had invested in a provincial company registered in Alberta and doing business in British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba, Ontario and Quebec. I think that some consideration should be given to the question of the names of these companies so that people who invest in them will know exactly what they are doing and that the name means something when they read it.

I should like to say something about this matter. I am glad that the hon. member for Kootenay West brought it up. I have not had an opportunity to consult with the sponsor of this bill, and I do not know that I would be in order if I were to move an amendment changing the name. I quite agree with the hon. member for Kootenay West that the present name might mislead a small speculator. You know, we are not all from St. James street or Bay street, or whatever the name is of the winding alley in Winnipeg. Some of us come from small country districts, and when we see the word Canada we are impressed.
Perhaps I could explain better this way. Some years ago a former member of this house sent out on our high-class House of Commons stationery a prospectus for an oil company, or perhaps it was a gold mine. I am glad to say he came from the other side of the house, but I am sorry to say he came from my province. There was the crest; there was the name Canada, and people with annuities or perhaps with small amounts of money to invest would buy those shares in good faith as a result. I am not saying for a moment that this is not a genuine company. I have no doubt that in time it will be very successful. In the meantime, however, we should not do anything that might mislead people out in the hinterland, such as those in Comox-Alberni, where very few people have had much experience in finance.
I do not want to take up much time on this bill, but I understand that in this very chamber a great deal of time was taken to discuss the question of whether the word "cola" could be used with the word "Pepsi"

in a trade mark. I believe, as the hon. member for Kootenay West says, the people of Canada should be fully protected at least until such time as this company has a dominion charter. Perhaps the company could secure the charter and later have their name changed to the Reinsurance Company of Canada Limited, in order to get it all in; but first they should obtain a dominion charter. I believe we should take a Tittle time to consider such an important matter as this. I am not allowed to refer to the other sections now, but there are sections of this bill which would not mean half as much to the investing public of Canada as the name of the company, particularly those not well advised on finance. I took some advice on stocks from a learned colleague who is well up in finance. He is well up, and now I am well down, having taken his advice. In that case I was acting on his judgment, and in this case small investors may act on the strength of the name.
As I have said already, there is a great deal of merit in the suggestion of the hon. member for Kootenay West. That is usually the case; he comes from a very fine province. So I think the house should pay particular attention to what he says. I do not want to delay this bill or to delay the committee longer, so I will only repeat that I concur entirely in the remarks of the hon. member for Kootenay West.
May I ask the sponsor in which provinces it is proposed to register this company?
I understand it is proposed to register it in the dominion and in Ontario, but the business of insurance will be carried on in all the provinces.

I do not know whether or not the matter I have in mind was discussed on second reading. The name of this company is Mercantile and General Reinsurance Company of Canada Limited:, but I can see nothing in the bill which would suggest that the business of the company is to be confined to reinsurance. This bill gives the company the right to carry on all kinds of insurance. I believe the general public would consider a reinsurance company to be particularly strong; that is the impression one gets. The weaker companies take out insurance and reinsure with stronger companies. Many companies, for example, reinsure with Lloyd's, and the name of this company conveys the impression that here we have a company somewhat similar to strong companies such as Lloyd's, doing a reinsurance business. When we look at the bill we see that the paid up capital is not very large; yet the impression

Private Bills
conveyed is that this is a strong company with great assets, large reserves and large capital, doing a reinsurance business. I do not think that impression should be conveyed by the name of a company which is just starting business, with a limited capital and with the paid up capital only a quarter of the total authorized by this bill.
I suggest that is a point to which the committee might be well advised to give some attention. From time to time over the years we have had difficulties with the names of insurance companies. Perhaps the sponsor of the bill can say something to put my mind at rest in this connection, but as the matter stands at the moment I would be inclined to oppose adoption of the bill until such time as we have some further explanation or even a new name, which would remove what seems to me an objectionable feature of the bill.

The hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar is quite correct in his interpretation of section 6 of the bill, in which the powers of the company are not limited to reinsurance. I am informed, and I can inform the committee, that in the beginning the company intends to conduct a reinsurance business solely, but they do not wish to limit their powers to reinsurance because as time goes on they intend to carry on other types of insurance as well.

The point I had in mind was exactly what the hon. member says, that this does suggest that the company is going to engage in general insurance. There is nothing in the bill which says its business will be only that of reinsurance, and that is the point I am making. The powers granted in this bill are those which would be granted to a company doing a general insurance business, and there is no mention anywhere of reinsurance, whether the initial business will be in reinsurance or whether it will be in general insurance. On the other hand there is every indication that the company intends to engage in a general insurance business. It is for that reason also, having in mind the amount of capital in the bill, it seems to me there is an objectionable feature in the name, reinsurance.

Mr. Chairman, as has been pointed out previously, one insurance company went bankrupt and caused a great deal of hardship to a great many people throughout Canada. As has been pointed out by the member for Rosetown-Biggar, in my opinion at least the name is misleading. What protection has an individual, not an investor in the capital of the company, but a policyholder in the insurance company? For instance, before we had such an excellent staff

as we have in charge of finance at Ottawa, we had a bank failure. Thousands of people in the Kootenays lost money, and I should like to know what protection there is. As I understand it, this company is going to carry on a general insurance business with a capital of $250,000. There are many individuals in the province of British Columbia who are insured for four or five times that amount. Of course, I will admit that is only one year's profit, but I should like the sponsor of the bill to tell us whether policyholders of this company will have the same protection as policyholders of the operating companies now have?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Since the Department of Finance has been mentioned, I should say that federal incorporation, of course, does include supervision by the federal superintendent of insurance. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a word on the point of order. I should like to draw to your attention the fact that the language that was used by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) is to be found in citation 323 of Beauchesne, third edition:

tne debate, for Instance, could make any amendments he desired to make; and we hope that he will make amendments. Mr. Speaker, I shall be brief in what I have to say. In dealing with the matter of this motion, I think the particular purpose we should have in view is to protect the right of the sponsor of the bill. I agree that that should be done. What would his position be if, the next time this bill comes up for discussion, the sponsor is here and the mover of the adjournment is not here? Will the bill stand over until he is here? I wish to thank hon. members for bringing to my attention these points, which are very pertinent to the point of order. I must admit that this question has given me some concern. I realize that the rights not only of the sponsor of the bill but of the hon. member who moved the amendment, and of all hon. members, must be protected. I did make a ruling on this matter on Friday, June 23, 1950, which was to the effect that when the sponsor of a private bill is not in the house the debate on that bill cannot proceed without his consent.
Tonight we have a case where the sponsor of a bill has requested, through another member, that the bill should stand. Now it has been suggested that because there is an amendment, the debate on the amendment should proceed, and that the mover of the amendment might be injured by not proceeding with the amendment. Therefore, he is not being injured in any way in that respect. Am I wrong? Notwithstanding, I will say that I have always considered that a private member who in sponsoring a bill stands in the same position as a member of the government who introduces a bill in the house. As hon. members know, when a government bill is introduced, it is introduced by a minister. There may be an amendment to that bill introduced by a private member. The discussion either on the bill or on the amendment does not proceed without the consent of the minister who introduced the bill. Why should a private member not stand in the same position? That has been the attitude that I have taken, and although I realize that it might appear that an injustice is being done, nevertheless I feel that I should not change the ruling which I made on Friday, June 23.
It has been said that the bill is now in the possession of the house, and that the amendment is in the possession of the house. Speaking to the point
of order as to whether the amendment is in order or not, I regret I must inflict on the house another discussion on a point of order. I am not speaking on the amendment or its merits. I would submit, sir, that the practice dealing with the handling in this house of private bills is clearly set out in the standing orders and the citations in that part of Beau-chesne, third edition, dealing with private bills; and further that the practice based on these standing orders and these citations is now established in this house by custom as well as by law.
In support of that statement I would refer Your Honour to citation 769, the appropriate part of which reads:
The expediency of a private bill, being mainly founded upon allegations of fact, which have not yet been proved, the house, in agreeing tp its second reading, affirms the principle of the bill, conditionally, and subject to the proof of such allegations before the committee.
It is the established practice in this house, according to the rule, that at the second reading the house will consider and pass upon the principle of the bill; that the committee to which the bill is referred under the appropriate standing order will be the judge of the facts upon which the application of the principle will or will not be based; in other words, the bill will or will not be passed. That process is set out in our own standing orders. What this amendment is asking the house to do is to put the cart before the horse, to reverse its own established procedure and to decide upon the facts before coming to a conclusion upon the principle of the bill. That I submit, Mr. Speaker, it cannot do.
It has been said by some hon. member-
I regret that I cannot credit him by name because I forget who it was-that the standing orders and the citations are there for our guidance, and that the least we can do is to fMr Speaker.]

try to be consistent in living up to them. Citations following citation 769-there are several of them-I put on the record at the time that I introduced the bill for second reading, and I do not intend to inflict them on the house again; but I will submit, sir, that they all carry out definitely the principle that I have tried to outline.
There is in Beauchesne, third edition, which is the last word on parliamentary procedure in so far as we are concerned, a special chapter entitled "Private Bills", and a section of the "Standing Orders" dealing with private bills. That is the chapter, these are the standing orders, these are the citations which must govern us at the moment.
I said, sir, that Beauchesne, third edition, is the last word which we have to refer to in matters of procedure. Beauchesne, in his third edition, quotes on several occasions with reference to private bills-and quotes with approval-Dodd and Wilberforce on "Private Bills Procedure", which says at page 20:
The house does not profess to decide upon the second reading as to the truth or otherwise of the allegations of fact upon which a proposed bill is based, and in conceding a second reading to a private bill the house is regarded as merely giving its sanction to its general principle on the hypothesis that the committee to which it afterwards is referred finds those allegations proved.
In Beauchesne we find citation 659 which reads in part as follows, after setting out at some length a case which was brought for decision:
The Speaker ruled this amendment out of order because it did not challenge the principle of the bill and it anticipated the committee stage.
That citation is in the part of Beauchesne which deals with public bills. I submit it is much more impressive when considered in conjunction with standing orders and citations dealing with private bills, as the amendment before the house does not oppose the principle of the bill and does attempt to anticipate the correct committee stage.
On anticipation, at page 273 of the Journals of the house for 1934 Mr. Speaker of that day, in ruling out of order an amendment proposed by the late Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, said:
The amendment moved by the right hon. leader of the opposition does not challenge the principle of Bill 51 and it anticipates the committee stage.
And then Mr. Speaker at a later point closed his ruling with these words:
The objections raised in the proposed amendment cannot be looked upon as reasons why Bill 51 should not now be proceeded with and, moreover, they may be considered after the bill has been read a second time.
Under our established practice the matters which the hon. member for Cape Breton

South wishes considered not only can but must be considered after the bill has been read the second time.
I should like to admit that there are in Beauchesne several citations which would indicate that a motion of this sort is entirely in order. But I would point out that those citations are not, any of them, to be found in that chapter or section of the book which deals with private bills, for which an entirely different practice is set out and has been established.
As to this may I read, with respect, from page 235 of the Journals of last year in which Mr. Speaker said:
Private bills are of a different nature from public bills. I have said that previously in the house. The principle of a private bill is approved conditionally on second reading, subject to confirmation upon satisfactory proof when the bill is before the committee.
As the Prime Minister has so well pointed out, standing order 104 makes it obligatory to refer a private bill, once it has received second reading, to one of the standing committees.
I submit that as to the practice there can be no question. There remains only the incident brought to the attention of the house by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who said, with perfect truth, that a motion in exactly the same terms as this, on a private bill in 1948, was submitted to the house and was voted upon. The record of this is to be found at page 2831 of Hansard for 1948. What actually occurred was that the hon. member moved his amendment and sat down, and Mr. Speaker took the vote. No question was raised as to whether or not the amendment was in order. Then are we bound by something which occurred in the house when no ruling was made and no point of order was raised? I think that was answered by the decision of Mr. Speaker, from which I quote briefly as it appears at page 215 of the Journals for 1950, where it says:
One must give the member for Winnipeg North, Centre (Mr. Knowles) full credit for finding an instance in 1891 when two such motions without intermediate proceedings were allowed. I repeat, however, that the Speaker did not make a ruling.
That is the end of the quotation. Therefore Mr. Speaker felt that he was not bound.
It would be unthinkable that we should be bound by the incident of 1948. An irregularity, even with the greatest vigilance, may easily slip through and occur once in the proceedings of this house, without a point of order being raised. I do not think it should be suggested that that would establish a precedent which would have the effect of overruling the standing orders and established practice of the house, as it has been over the years. I submit that the amendment is completely out of order on a private bill.

Mr. Chairman, in view of the fact that, following the discussions and rulings of last Thursday, the discussion now is ranging broadly over the eight sections of the resolution, may I direct a question to the parliamentary assistant with reference to item No. 3, the proposed reduction in the excise tax on candy, chocolate, chewing gum and confectionery from 30 per cent to 15 per cent. The reasons for this proposed reduction have been indicated by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech. It strikes me if these reasons are valid, and I have no reason to think they are not, that the proper course for the government to have followed would have been not simply to propose a reduction in the tax but repeal of the tax. I ask the parliamentary assistant, therefore, particularly in the light of the statement made by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech of April 10, what justification there can be for continuing this tax even at the 15 per cent rate?

Before the parliamentary
assistant answers, may I suggest to the hon. member for Eglinton that he should visit the plants of manufacturers of candy and chocolate. He would be surprised to see the number of machines that were idle on account of the heavier tax. I took the trouble to visit a big plant in Montreal. I will give the name to my hon. friend if he wants it. I was surprised to see the number of machines that they had to make and wrap chocolate bars. The only thing that was done by hand was the putting of chocolate drops into the boxes. It is a huge plant that has to be enlarged, and I was surprised at the number of machines that were idle. I asked about the personnel, and they told me that the number of personnel was one-quarter of what is was in August of last year. They said that in August of last year they had 600 people working there, and the number had fallen to 200. This was before Easter, the busy season for candy manufacturers.
I had a letter from a candy manufacturer in my constituency who told me that he would have to close his business if the tax was maintained at 30 per cent. The same thing was said by many other candy and chocolate manufacturers, and I am sure that the minister had representations from all over the country to the same effect. When I was in Toronto I would have liked to visit the Neilson plant, but I did not have the time to do so because we were so busy seeing interesting things. I would have made a point to go there and ask them if conditions were the same in their plant as they were in the plant of the Montreal candy manufacturers. When hundreds of people are put out 80709-165

of work precisely on account of the increase in the tax, I find it judicious of the government to decrease the tax in order to give more employment to people.
My hon. friend knows what quantities of chocolate bars are sold to children, and not only to children but to people who travel and eat them on trains, and to people who eat them at picnics, and so on. The consumption is very large in Canada. It is true that they are a good food but that is not my point. What I wanted to tell my hon. friend, and what I want the hon. gentleman to understand, is that it is not a matter of producing more candy. It is not so much that as the idea of keeping people at work who are accustomed to doing that type of work, women who cannot do hard work. Moreover, if my hon. friend takes the time to go to Neilson's in Toronto, a firm that I have not visited, and others in other cities of Canada, he will be surprised to see the machines they use for the manufacture of chocolates and other candy, and I am sure he will appreciate the fact that the tax has been reduced as much as possible in order to provide more work for both men and women.

May I remind the committee that a similar tax was in effect until the spring of 1949. The pre-election budget was distinguished among other things by the entire repeal of this same tax. The repeal lasted only until September, 1950, when the Minister of Finance, even in the face of the reasons which he had given in the spring of 1949 for repeal of this tax, asked the house to reimpose the tax and to levy it at the rate of 30 per cent. In his budget speech on April 10 the minister said, as reported at page 1812 of Hansard:
In September a tax of 30 per cent was imposed on all candy, confectionery and chewing gum. Experience has shown that this rate has been too severe, and its effects upon the industry have been out of proportion in comparison with other taxed industries. We propose, therefore, to reduce this rate to 15 per cent.
In that brief reference, Mr. Chairman, I think the minister has shown quite conclusively what were the inherent defects of this tax. First of all, it was discriminatory. It singled! out the manufacturers of a particular article or articles, which in the eyes of most people are a food', for a special tax. As the hon. member for Temiscouata has pointed out, in that respect it was discriminatory against the persons employed by the companies producing these goods as well as against those who were employers and industrialists. In the second place, the minister has pointed out that the tax had a damaging effect on the industry. He drew attention to the fact that the effects on the

Excise Tax Act
industry have been out of all proportion in comparison with other taxed industries. The amount realized from this type of tax, which of course in large measure is paid by youngsters and the parents of youngsters, has been out of all proportion to the damage which has been done to the industry and consumers.
I come back to the question I put to the parliamentary assistant. If the Minister of Finance has given sound reasons for the proposed reduction in the tax, it seems he has given equally sound reasons for its complete repeal, and I ask what justification there can be for continuing to tax even at the rate of 15 per cent.

This is the first time I have taken part in any of the discussions concerning the budget, but I feel I must say something in opposition to the increase in the sales tax. In his budget speech the minister said, in mentioning this increase-I am not quoting his words but giving their sense or import- that as 95 per cent of the food items were exempt from the sales tax, for that reason this tax would not fall heavily on those in the low income brackets. That seems to me terribly callous reasoning. Surely people whose incomes are already so low that the greater part must be spent on food are sufficiently punished even if they go free of all taxes.
Then on Thursday evening, I think it was, the parliamentary assistant referred to the fact that the number of persons gainfully employed in this country was 5,200,000, but of that number only 2,200,000 paid income tax. I do not know whether he said in effect that the reason for this increase in the sales tax was to catch the other 3,000,000 so that they would contribute to paying for some of the social services they enjoy. Let us examine that reasoning. If the reasoning of the Minister of Finance was callous this is equally callous, if not more so. The exemptions under the Income Tax Act are $1,000 for a single person and $2,000 for a married person.

For example, $125 million is the figure which we are raising by the increase in tax. When the amendment to one of the clauses was before the committee a little earlier, I pointed out, just by a quick examination of the figures put on record by the minister, that this would have necessitated the substitution of an increased liquor

tax, which is already a very high one, from $12 a gallon to $36 a gallon, assuming that there was absolutely no diminution in the rate of consumption. It is considerations like that which the minister has detailed in the speech itself, as he examines the revenue he can raise from each of the major fields, which led him to that conclusion. If the minister with his logic cannot persuade the hon. member of the correctness of his case, certainly he cannot expect me to do so. As to the hon. member for Eglinton-
May I just make one observation before the parliamentary assistant leaves his reference to me?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I should prefer to go through and finish.
That is fine.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I waited until several members had made their points, which I noted. The hon. member for Red Deer insisted that I get to my feet. Now that I have risen, I think that I should at least be allowed to finish my remarks and deal with the other points.
I can make my observations later.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The hon. member for Eglinton referred to the tax on candy. Since we had found that this taxation on candy was too heavy in relation to taxation in competing fields, he asks why we did not remove it completely. Of course, I cannot quite follow his logic. Because the tax is too heavy, that does not imply immediately that the whole tax should be removed. We have reduced it to 15 per cent. We have cut it in half. The candy and chocolate manufacturers naturally would be happy-as would any other manufacturer-to see all taxes on their product totally removed. But as the hon. member for Charlotte has pointed out, their feeling is that this action would put them in a position where they can again compete.
The points put forward by the hon. member for Vancouver East, of course, have been put forward by practically every other opposition member who spoke. The point made by the hon. member for Red Deer this afternoon, to the effect that people in opposition talk differently about the sales tax from people in government, is of course amply borne out by the records which have already been presented in this house. When the Conservatives increased the sales tax 500 per cent, from one per cent to six per cent, of course the Liberals were indignant. Now the Conservatives are equally indignant because, as a result of defence revenue needs, we have been forced to increase it 25 per

cent, from eight per cent to ten per cent. The hon. member for Vancouver East of course will recall that the C.C.F. in power feel differently about the sales tax from the C.C.F. not in power, because in Saskatchewan, I understand, despite the promises to remove the sales tax when they were in opposition, the sales tax has been increased by the C.C.F. government from two per cent to three per cent, which is a 50 per cent increase.

But they removed it from a long list of the necessities of life-from foods, meals, drugs and a long list of other things. As far as the C.C.F. here are concerned, may I say that we have not changed our opinion.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Of course not. That is the whole point of the little argument I am making. When they are in opposition, of course it is an iniquitous tax. I am amazed that the leader of the C.C.F. should have so little influence on the provincial government in Saskatchewan.
I have no more to do with the provincial government in Saskatchewan than has the Prime Minister to do with the provincial government, we will say, of Nova Scotia or of Quebec.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I should think it was important that the one socialist government in Canada would be a model government, and that the leader of the C.C.F. group would take more than a paternal interest in what they were doing.
As to the list of exemptions, our list of exemptions to the sales tax is a far wider one than any provincial list of exemptions in any of the provinces which apply the sales tax.
Since you, Mr. Chairman, permitted the hon. member for Vancouver East to extend his argument on the income tax, may I say that the point I made, by raising the fact that out of 5,200,000 people gainfully employed in Canada only 2,200,000 paid income tax last year, was in order to point out with the tables that in Canada we give the highest income tax exemptions of any country of the western world. It is not that our incomes are too low, but rather that we have seen to it that our income tax exemptions are the highest of any in the western world. When I get to the income tax resolution, I will certainly put on the record the income tax exemptions of other countries and the actual taxes paid by a Canadian earning $3,000 a year.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
