speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, if I used the word "permit". In any case, like the hon. member for Vancouver East, I have now finished that avenue.
One other point raised as to the tax on candies was that it was not only the tax on candy but the large increase in the cost of raw cocoa beans which has also affected our Canadian chocolate manufacturers. That situation of course was mentioned by the hon. member for Charlotte. The other evening the hon. member for St. John's West asked me about the customs tariffs on these various items. I have that information with me tonight and when we are on the customs tariff bill I will give it to him.
May I just ask one question here? Is it not a fact that imported chocolates also pay the excise tax; that is, they pay the customs tariff and the excise tax?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is quite true.
I understood the hon. member for Charlotte to say that it was unfair competition from the British chocolate candy manufacturers about which they were complaining. Perhaps I misunderstood him.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No. The hon. member's point was that the chocolate manufacturers in Britain can buy their cocoa beans at a better price than can our Canadian manufacturer. The source of cocoa beans is the Gold Coast of west Africa; and cocoa is subsidized in Britain.
May I pursue this matter, Mr. Chairman? The parliamentary assistant's answer to my question was interesting but not very convincing.
It was not an answer at all.

One could hardly construe it as an answer. When on a previous occasion I referred to my conviction that the budget had been thrown together in a hurry, I was making specific reference to the specific proposals contained in it. But I assumed at least that the minister would be extremely careful with regard to the use of words in trying to deal with a set of proposals which must have been a bit unwholesome even to him in his way of thinking. In the second place, Mr. Chairman, it is obvious that the parliamentary assistant undertook to convey the impression that I was suggesting that if he had not acquired $100 million from an increase in the sales tax, he would have had

Excise Tax Act
to procure it from additional taxes on one other commodity, and he mentioned liquor. I suggested earlier in the debate that I was convinced that the minister was not limited to liquor. In fact, I made one or two other suggestions. I would say there are a great many fields open. The effect of my question was to question the propriety of indicating to this house that he was limited to a choice of one of two things. Personally, I am convinced that he was limited to no such field at all. As I see it, I think it was a mere attempt to find an additional argument, if possible, for doing something which the minister knew would be most unpopular with the Canadian people.
I just wish to make one other reference. The parliamentary assistant referred to an observation of mine this afternoon with regard to a Liberal member acting one way when he is a member of the opposition and acting in quite another way when he is a member of the government. I had in mind this: In the late spring and early summer of 1935 when the Liberals were asserting to all who would listen that they were certain to form the next government, they were also damning the sales tax. Yet, when they brought down their first budget on May 1, 1936, one of the first things they did was to increase the sales tax from 6 per cent to 8 per cent, and estimate that they would draw from the pockets of the people $23 million additional tax by that process. It seems rather strange to me that such things could all occur within the space of less than a year.	The sales taxes were vicious in
principle in the late spring of 1935 and during the summer, and particularly during the election campaign of the fall of 1935. It is an amazing thing that it took on such favourable characteristics almost immediately after the Liberals were elected to office, and more particularly when the minister of finance of that date was drafting his budget. But I do not intend to say anything more, Mr. Chairman, except to reassert that I should have liked to get a list of those factors which limited the minister in his choice between increasing the income tax on the one hand, and imposing a sales tax on the other; but obviously I shall not get a more specific answer tonight, and therefore I will let it ride at that.

I should like to bring up the matter of sales tax on school busses. I know that the Minister of Finance has received representations from the Alberta school trustees association, and I think from a large number of other school associations in connection with the sales tax, requesting that it be removed so far as busses and other

vehicles used solely for the purpose of transporting pupils to and from schools are concerned.
We have in this house a considerable number of debates in connection with federal aid to education. Nothing has been done along that line. This is one of the ways in which the federal government could give a certain amount of aid to education without hurting themselves to any extent. It seems an unreasonable thing that the school districts and municipal areas throughout the province should be burdened when they are attempting to raise the money to finance schools; and as for the busses they purchase for that purpose, or busses used for that purpose in the school district-they have to pay it eventually whether they actually own the busses or somebody else does-it seems quite ridiculous that these municipal areas should have to pay the sales tax on busses used for this purpose or other vehicles used solely for this purpose.
Last year I brought this same matter up, and the minister promised to give consideration to it in the following year's budget-that is, the present budget we are considering. Apparently nothing has been included. Why has the sales tax on these school busses not been done away with? Is the parliamentary assistant going to answer?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I have been answering
questions in batches for three or four members at a time. I did that to save time, but if hon. members want me to answer them individually, all right.

Then I have another
question that I also submitted to the Minister of Finance some time ago. It is in connection *with the sales tax on gasoline-powered vehicles, trucks and so forth, which are used exclusively in the production of coal. There is an anomalous situation in this connection. Any truck, or other vehicle, which is a diesel-powered vehicle and used exclusively in the production of coal does not bear sales tax; but if the motor in the truck-it might be exactly the same truck-is a gasoline-powered motor it is subject to sales tax. It does exactly the same work, and the request that was made to the minister in this connection was that gasoline-powered vehicles used exclusively in the production of coal, chiefly in stripping operations-there are some vehicles also used in mines-be not subject to the sales tax. I have in front of me a letter from the minister in which he says: "I shall be very pleased to consider this request when I am reviewing the sales tax proposals during preparation of the budget." Well, apparently he was pleased

to consider it, but there does not seem to have been any action. Why has that change in the sales tax set-up not been made? The amount of money which would be lost to the federal government as a result of repealing this tax would be very small. The number of these vehicles used is not great, but so far as the people in the business are concerned it is quite an important item. In view of the fact that this concession was made so far as diesel-powered trucks are concerned, I can really see no reason, no sense from any point of view, why gasoline-powered trucks should not be put in the same position.

May I also take this
opportunity of saying thank you to the department and the minister for reducing the tax from 30 per cent to 15 per cent on candy goods. I should like to bring to the attention of this committee something that was happening in my riding to a small firm that was attempting to carry on business, and the way in which this 30 per cent tax adversely affected not only the business but the income of the government as well. To that end I shall quote from a letter received from the Tweed chamber of commerce:
At a recent meeting of Tweed chamber of commerce, it was disclosed that the 30 per cent excise tax, recently imposed by the dominion government on certain types of confections, has resulted in a serious blow to one of Tweed's leading industries, the W. T. Hawkins Company, Limited.
They are manufacturers of caramel-coated' popcorn, which is now affected by the tax. Since the tax was imposed, employees are only working part time and as a result a great deal less money from the company's payroll is in circulation in the village.
If the purpose of the government was toward increased revenues, it is quite clear that the tax has had the exact opposite effect in the case of the Hawkins company, where production has been reduced by 75 per cent.
Tweed chamber of commerce looks on the tax as a serious threat to business among the merchants in our community. We would greatly appreciate it if you would kindly bring to the attention of the government the damaging effect that the tax has had on business in this little town.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I should like to go further and show by a comparison the effect that this 30 per cent tax has had not only on the business of this company but on the income of the government as well. The average monthly sales for twelve months ended October 30, 1950, before the tax was put on was $22,359. After the tax was imposed the average monthly sales for five months ended February 28, 1951, was $5,724. The average monthly sales tax for twelve months ended September 30, 1950, was $1,788. The average monthly taxes, sales tax and) excise tax, for five months ended February 28, 1951, were $2,190. During that time the cost of
Excise Tax Act
ingredients and packing materials of course increased as well. This company was faced not only with declining sales but increased cost. The ingredients such as corn increased from October, 1949, to February, 1951, 19-8 per cent; sugar increased in the same period 19-1 per cent; corn syrup, 14-8 per cent; cellophane bags for packing, 17-4 per cent; display boxes, 28-2 per cent and' cases for packing, 14-5 per cent.
This product is one known as Caramel Corn Snacks, and I submit the government should consider that this com should be treated in the same way as other popcorn, should be declared outside the act and be made tax free.
On a resume of the net sales I would point out the figures from July 1950 to February' 1951. In July of 1950 the net sales amounted to $22,555.77, while the total sales and excise taxes amounted to $1,804.07. In August of that year the net sales amounted to $19,508.24, while the total sales and excise taxes amounted to $1,560.66. In September, the net sales amounted to $14,903.68, while the income to the government from sales and excise taxes amounted to $4,374.63. Then when the 30 per cent tax went on, in October the sales dropped to $5,247.66, and the income to the government in sales and excise taxes amounted to $1,994.11. In November the net sales was valued at $9,864.77, whereas the total sales and excise taxes amounted to $3,748.61. In November sales were higher, owing to the sale of a new 25-cent package, in the hope that it would stem the falling off of business. However, most of those 25cent packages are still in the hands of distributors, and' unsold at the present time. In December net sales amounted to $5,019.82, and total sales and' excise taxes to $1,907.54. Then, in January of 1951, net sales were valued at $5,539.33 whereas total sales and excise taxes amounted to $2,104.95. In February, total sales amounted in $3,148.60 whereas total sales and excise taxes amounted to $1,196.47. Once again I would impress upon the government the fact that this product is similar to that now being marketed as a candy cereal, on which there is no tax. It is in direct competition with popcorn, which, as I have said, apparently is outside the act and is not subject to tax.
I would ask the parliamentary assistant to take the matter into consideration and to pass on to his minister the request that this caramel product, known as Snacks, be placed on a basis comparable with popcorn, and thus be declared tax free.

I should like to ask two questions, the first of which has to do with the

Excise Tax Act
application of the sales tax on motor cars. Representations have been made to me respecting a person who had paid for his car in Vancouver, and was to take delivery at the factory in the east. He was to pick up his car on April 18. Meantime the tax was announced, and he has been charged the increased percentage.
My second question has to do with a new drug known as Chloromycetin, which apparently is subject to the sales tax at the present time. This drug is very expensive, twenty pills costing about $16. I believe it falls into the category of a necessity in connection with the treatment of a certain type of ailment. The parliamentary assistant knows that in many cases people who require these drugs have already suffered greatly from sickness, and are in poor financial circumstances. Is there any possibility of having this drug included among the exceptions? If it were so included the amount of tax lost would be negligible, and I believe a genuine case has been made for those who must use it. The person who wrote to me had to take one of these pills every four hours for at least three days. The parliamentary assistant will see that at a price of $16 for twenty pills this runs into heavy expense. Could this drug be included among those already mentioned in the resolution?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The hon, member for Calgary East asked why the sales tax had not been removed from school busses. Two years ago we removed the excise tax from such busses, and at that time the move was naturally welcomed. School busses in this country fall into two categories. The great bulk of them are not owned by school boards, but are owned rather by men in the transportation business. In my own riding, for example, the busses are privately owned and used for other purposes during the day. The difficulty of establishing a hard and clear line between a bus company which pays not only the sales tax but also the 25 per cent excise tax, and which has not a school bus franchise, and those who have a school bus franchise, would make it a very difficult problem of administration. We have given relief to the extent that school busses do not pay the excise tax on motor cars.
The second point raised by the hon. member was as to why we still levy the sales tax on gasoline-powered equipment used by mines or quarries for off-road work. The exemption of diesel-powered equipment is fairly recent. The mining industry welcomed it as a great step forward. Diesel equipment is, of course, larger, more expensive and heavier than gasoline-powered equipment.
It has far less other uses. Most gasoline-powered equipment can be converted quickly to other uses, and in this respect is unlike the diesel-powered equipment. If hon. members will look at the customs tariff schedule they will see that we are again widening very greatly the tariff concessions on mining equipment.
I might add that this distinction between diesel-powered and gasoline-powered equipment is not confined to mining and quarrying. In the same customs tariff amendments it will be found that we exempt diesels used by fishermen, whereas gasoline-powered equipment used by fishermen is still subject to the tariff.
Then the hon. member for Hastings South raised the point he had already raised with the department with respect to the tax on candy-coated popcorn. Once again this raises the problem as to where the borderline in taxation must go. In his mind he can build up good reason as to why this product should be subject only to the tax applicable to nuts and popcorn. Of course the candy people would be the first to complain by saying that here is a candy-coated confection free from tax being sold in competition with candy which is paying 15 per cent. They would ask that since this confection is candy-coated it should be classed as a candy.
The actual budget resolution refers to candy, chocolate, chewing gum and confec- ' tionery that may be classed as candy or a substitute for candy. I know that the average small child who buys candy-coated popcorn feels that he or she is buying candy, not popcorn. For that reason they are included in that category, and I feel sure that the remission of the excise tax from 30 per cent to 15 per cent will be helpful to the firm the hon. member has mentioned.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has raised the matter as to when the sales tax on cars applies. It has been the ruling of the Department of National Revenue that the sales tax applies on delivery from the manufacturer. Some sales dealers do sell cars ahead of time on contract, that they will sell the car at a certain price, no matter what tax change may take place. In that case the dealer must pay the increased tax, if any.
Then, so far as the special drug the hon. member mentioned is concerned, my answer would be that we have to be pretty well guided by the regulations of the Department of National Health and Welfare. The question of taxation of drugs is a different one because there are many drugs, some very expensive and some cheap, some which of course are
:Wr. Green.]

well known and very useful and others concerning which doctors have doubts as to their effectiveness despite the enthusiasm with which individuals may use them. If this drug has a widespread use and is as expensive as it is said to be, I have no doubt that the Department of National Health and Welfare will make representations to the department to include it, perhaps not this time but for next year's budget, with the class of drugs under doctors' prescriptions which we now exempt from sales tax.

Mr. Chairman, I think the parliamentary assistant rather sought to brush aside what had been said with respect to the inadequacy of the reduction in the tax on candy, chocolate and confectionery. I think the point is not to be so easily avoided, that the Minister of Finance himself has in effect destroyed by his argument any basis in logic for continuing this tax even at the reduced rate. Bear in mind, sir, that this form of product bears a sales tax. What we are dealing with here is an excise tax in addition to the general sales tax which itself is going to be increased by the present budget. Let us not overlook that.
When hon. Liberal members, two of whom have spoken tonight, commend the Minister of Finance for reducing the excise tax on candy, chocolate and confectionery, let us bear in mind at the same time that the increase in the sales tax on the same commodities is going to have the effect of largely neutralizing this inadequate reduction in the excise tax. I am sure I do not need to spend any time in answering the argument that no reduction is required because two government supporters in the house tonight have already given a rather graphic picture of the very harmful effects experienced by the manufacturers of these commodities and their employees as a result of the very drastic excise tax of 30 per cent that was applied last September on those commodities.
I happen to have some figures here indicating the increased costs which have confronted the manufacturers of these commodities. I have the figures of the cost of their raw materials in 1939 and alongside them the figures of the cost of their raw materials in 1950 at the time the minister applied his 30 per cent excise tax. I shall indicate in each case the proportion of increase for each item of raw material that enters into the production of candy, chocolate and confectionery. The first is cocoa beans. The price in 1939 was 7 cents a pound and in 1950 38 cents a pound, an increase of 443 per cent. The price of cocoa butter in 1939 was 14-9 cents a pound, and in 1950 80 cents a pound, an
Excise Tax Act
increase of 437 per cent. The price of sugar in 1939 was 5 cents a pound, and in 1950 9-66 cents a pound, an increase of 93 per cent. While I am speaking about sugar, let me remind the committee, Mr. Chairman, that a special excise tax is collected on sugar.
The raw material cost of glucose in 1939 was 3'35 cents a pound, and in 1950 7-07 cents a pound, an increase of 111 per cent. The price of milk powder in 1939 was 13-82 cents a pound, and in 1950 28-42 cents a pound, an increase of 105 per cent. Turning for the moment from raw materials to paper and packaging materials of various kinds, the increase in the period from 1939 to 1950 has been variously from 50 per cent to 75 per cent. As to peanuts, which enter into the production of a good deal of confectionery, in 1939 the price was 5 cents a pound, and in 1950 15 cents a pound, an increase of 300 per cent. Then there is also the increase in labour costs which from 1939 to 1950 show an increase of 65 to 100 per cent depending upon the nature of the particular work.
In the face of these heavy increases in the cost of production, this industry, which has suffered seriously under the handicap imposed by the minister in his 30 per -cent tax last fall, is, on the minister's own reasoning as disclosed in the budget speech, entitled to something better than a 15 per cent decrease in the excise tax while at the same time facing an increase from 8 per cent to 10 per cent in the sales tax. Anything that the parliamentary assistant has said on the subject tonight seems to me to fall far short of justifying the inadequacy of this decrease, or in fact any continuance of the excise tax on these commodities at all. So much for the one decrease in taxes offered by the budget.
The rest of the picture is one of increases down the line. As to these increases I wish to make two observations of a general nature. In the first place it seems to me that it is axiomatic in all taxation that taxes ought not to be discriminatory, that they should not favour one group at the expense of another, that they should not penalize manufacturers or producers in one particular line while at the same time benefiting or exempting others in similar lines of production. That has been one of the main grounds of attack on and protest against the impositions in this budget. Let me take your mind back, Mr. Chairman, to last September when the Minister of Finance for no adequate reason chose to select certain commodities as targets for the imposition of what was then a 15 per cent excise tax. There were those who muttered the world "luxuries" under their breath and conjured up memories of the so-called luxury
2592

Excise Tax Act
tax that was imposed during the war, a tax, let me remind you, which was not imposed at the producer level but was a tax on the consumer. It was a tax levied at the point where the goods left the retailer to enter the hands of the consumer, a tax that was well known, well advertised, and which the people who were paying it had an opportunity to measure. The Minister of Finance in due time sought to replace that tax by a hidden tax, a more favoured form of taxation because it is thought to be easier to extract money out of people when they are not conscious of paying a tax on the commodities they have to buy. But when some were recalling that so-called luxury tax of war days, I do not recall that anyone in the house had the temerity to stand up in his place when this tax was under debate last September and say that the commodities upon which the minister then proposed to apply a 15 per cent excise tax were in fact luxuries. You have only to look at the list to realize that some of these articles are clearly articles in very common use in hundreds of thousands of households in this country. Articles such as toasters, electric kettles, electric irons, vacuum cleaners and so on were singled out for the imposition of this special 15 per cent excise tax. The unrepentant Minister of Finance is not satisfied with having discriminated against those who produce these articles, whether employers or employees, and against those who sell them and those who buy them; he has chosen to increase the tax from 15 per cent to 25 per cent in addition to the sales tax, which has also been increased by 25 per cent. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that there is no ground whatever for singling out commodities such as those for the application of this discriminatory tax.
Take luggage, for instance. I will concede at once that there are some very expensive types of luggage which in all fairness might well bear their share of necessary taxation, but there is a great deal of luggage that cannot be classified as luxuries by any stretch of the imagination. Therefore there can be no justification for singling out that type of luggage, first of all last September for the imposition of a 15 per cent excise tax, and now for an increase in that tax to 25 per cent accompanied by a 25 per cent increase in the sales tax.
If the minister wants to draw a line between what may be regarded* by most people as luxuries on the one hand and on the other hand those commodities, perhaps of a similar nature but less expensive, which most people would regard as reasonable necessities of life, let him do so; but let him not proceed, as he did last September and as

he is trying to do now, to select articles without making the slightest attempt to distinguish beween those that are luxuries on the one hand and those that are necessities on the other, and include them all in his discriminatory taxes.
It seems to me that in respect to the taxes under debate in this eight-point resolution the minister has offended that first canon of taxation, that there should be no discrimination, that taxation should be fair in its general incidence.
Another rule or canon of taxation I think the minister has woefully transgressed' in this resolution is that when the cost of living is rising rapidly, when the full effects of inflation are bearing oppressively on most of the people, if there must be increased' taxation the taxes imposed should not be such as to increase the inflationary pressures on the one hand or to take away from those upon whom these inflationary pressures are bearing most severely the limited means at their disposal to meet the soaring cost of living. In almost every respect this resolution concerning excise and sales taxes has offended in the most flagrant way that simple and obvious canon, though if ever there was a time when it should be observed it is in this year of inflation 1951.
What do we see? I have pointed out that in the sales tax, which applies to so many of the elementary necessities of life, the minister is imposing a 25 per cent increase. That is the most inflationary form of taxation being used as a fiscal weapon in the hands of the Minister of Finance today. Of all the taxes levied by the government the sales tax is the most inflationary; yet the minister has chosen to increase it by 25 per cent. All of a piece with that design is the increase to which I just referred^ from 15 per cent to 25 per cent, in the excise tax on a list of commodities many of which could not by any stretch of the imagination be regarded as luxuries.
Then, in a third offence against the simple and obvious rule of fair play with respect to taxation in times like these, the minister has chosen to sweep into the category of articles subject to a 15 per cent excise tax a range of commodities including washing machines, refrigerators and other things. These are not only necessities for great numbers of people; actually they enable many families to conserve food and reduce food costs. They have helped* many families reduce the domestic labour of the household, and have permitted more members of the family to engage in gainful employment at a time like this when an increase in the labour force is being

demanded from all sides. No one in touch with the realities of Canadian life could possibly justify increases in the taxes on such commodities as I have mentioned.
The suggestion has emanated) from government benches during the course of this debate that the scrub board is good enough for people in times such as these.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Who saidi that?
It has been mentioned by several hon. members in the course of the debate. If the parliamentary assistant will refresh his memory from Hansard he will see several references to the subject.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: You said it came from the government benches.

The proposal that commodities such as washing machines and so on should now be treated' as luxuries and subjected: to a 15 per cent tax, if it has any basis in reason or any thinking back of it, must have been prompted by the thought in the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite that the women in this country could do without those things because they are luxuries. If the government wants to split hairs on that they will have their opportunity. I do not think the people in this country will thank any government for suggesting that washing machines are not to be regarded as one of the household necessities of life in this country. Anyone who wants to adtvocate and approve the soaking of the housewife with a 15 per cent excise tax on a washing machine on top of a 25 per cent increase in the sales tax on the same commodity will have an opportunity during this debate to stand1 up and say that he gives his full assent to the shocking proposals that have emanated from the Minister of Finance.
Now, sir, the parliamentary assistant, in connection with the sales tax, and I think this form of reasoning might, if it has anything in it, apply to the excise tax as well, has sought to pass off the attack on this iniquitous increase in the sales tax by saying, "Oh, well, when people are in opposition they ask for a reduction in the sales tax, but when they get into the government they increase it.'' Since the last Conservative government in this country we have seen this government, in the election campaign in 1935 through the then leader of the opposition and the man who was shortly to become prime minister, denounce the sales tax as an iniquitous form of tax, then turn around as soon as it had power and increase the sales tax from six per cent to eight per cent. We are seeing the same mentality bearing further fruit now. But the parliamentary 80709-1661
Excise Tax Act
assistant in his remarks tonight missed something when he was talking about this and passing it off so lightly as being the sort of thing people object to when they are in opposition but support in increased form when they are in the government. He has overlooked the fact that two very eminent ministers of finance, when they were bearing responsibilities greater than those faced by the Minister of Finance today, in seeking revenues to meet the crisis of war deliberately refrained from increasing the sales tax. It was not a case of their being in opposition when they refused to increase the sales tax. They were in power and they deliberately rejected the temptation to increase the sales tax simply because of the ease with which it can be collected.
Mr. Ilsley, in April, 1941, a very dark time during the war, deliberately rejected any proposal for an increase in that tax, and he did so with these words:
An increase in the sales tax has, I think, been fairly generally expected. At least, there are evidences of a good deal of buying in anticipation of such an increase. This tax, while comparatively easy of administration and collection and extremely productive, has marked defects as a fiscal instrument. After extended consideration, we decided on balance against any increase. In coming to this decision, we were not forgetful of the problems of agriculture, which would have been intensified had the sales tax been raised.
Those are the serious words of Mr. Ilsley in 1941. What would Mr. Ilsley have to say if he were in this house today, faced with the degree of inflation that exists in the country, with the degree of elasticity which has appeared to an increasing extent in the Canadian dollar, the shrivelling of that dollar in the face of mounting costs of the things the housewife has to buy? What would he have had to say about the temptation to increase the sales tax simply because it is productive and easy to collect? Certainly, Mr. Ilsley, faced with a responsibility in 1941 greater than that facing the present minister, rejected all attempts to increase the sales tax.
Then, in February, 1945, the same Mr. Ilsley again deliberately rejected an increase in the sales tax. He referred to the fact that many of these taxes which are imposed far back on the production process increase costs out of proportion to the contributions which they make to the revenue.
In 1940 Mr. Ralston said:
We realize that increases in indirect taxes disguise the burdens imposed by the war but they are much more likely to distribute these burdens harshly and unfairly.
That is exactly what these proposed new taxes are going to do. They are going to distribute the burden of taxation harshly

Excise Tax Act
and unfairly, and they are going to accelerate the inflationary process. They are going to violate every plain rule that common sense would dictate with respect to the raising of revenue at a time of high inflation.
Finally, sir, on this subject of drugs, I am sure the house will welcome the seventh section in this resolution, which proposes to exempt two drugs from the sales tax, cortisone and ACTH. But, as has been pointed out, why stop there? Why, when the unfairness of imposing a sales tax on these two drugs is recognized by the Minister of Finance, would he continue to impose a sales tax, yes an increased sales tax of twenty-five per cent on the other range of drugs to which sales tax now applies? It seems to me the minister has, by the introduction of this item in the first resolution with respect to excise tax, condemned that act in so far as it either continues the present sales tax or increases the sales tax on another very wide range of drugs. In speaking last week on this resolution the member for Greenwood drew attention to at least one other drug about which I also have received some representations, and about which I know the minister has received representations. It is a drug that is known as prostigmin, and it is a necessity in the treatment of myasthenia gravis. That is just one, and there are many others that leap to the mind of each one of us here. Why should the sales tax, an increased sales tax, be imposed upon drugs which have to be purchased in large quantities by people who are chronic sufferers from diseases for which these drugs are prescribed.
Mr. Chairman, if the Minister of Finance withdrew this entire resolution with respect to the Excise Tax Act except for No. 7, he would be doing his bare minimum duty in the face of the hardships that the balance of the resolution will impose upon the Canadian people. The whole resolution, except No. 7, is shot through with discrimination. It will operate most unfairly on those who are least able to bear these heavy increases in taxation. Mr. Chairman, I urge upon all members of the house that it is our duty to resist this resolution, with the exception of No. 7, to the utter limit and to see to it that sufficient opposition from all parts of the house is mustered against this iniquitous proposal for increasing these heavy impositions that the Minister of Finance will see fit to withdraw this resolution, with the exception of item No. 7.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I should like to answer this immediately. I, of course, feel that this last speech has gone very far from the purpose of being in committee on the resolutions. When the general budget speech is made, of course members can speak generally on the

principles of the changes which have been announced. It has been my experience in the past that when we go into committee on the resolutions the purpose is to allow members to elicit more information about individual tax changes. Tonight we have heard for about the fourth time the full budget speech of the hon. member, mostly in generalities. He is better when he is indulging in generalities, as I shall show very quickly when I mention the two or three times in which he became specific.
Very early in his speech in connection with the candy tax, he said that we are taking off fifteen per cent excise tax then putting on two per cent sales tax, thus neutralizing the cut. I have a daughter eight years old, and even she knows that if you take fifteen off and put two back on, you are still thirteen to the good. Then he went on to make an even more amazing statement. He said there is still a special excise tax on sugar. As a Conservative, he would remember that there was an excise tax placed on sugar by R. B. Bennett. If there is one subject in recent years on which we have been hearing the hon. member speak at greater length than on this resolution, it is the famous radio budget of 1947. I was under the impression that the hon. member had either heard it or read it, but if he had he would certainly have remembered that on that occasion the Minister of Finance forecast the removal of the excise tax on sugar, which was confirmed the following session.
Then, he went on about discrimination. It was unfair to discriminate against any one industry by special taxation rates. Our whole tax structure since confederation has had varying rates of taxation against various industries. Today, for example, we have a 25 per cent tax on cosmetics. As I pointed out earlier, we have today, jointly with the provinces, an effective rate of about 300 per cent on liquor. Already this session the hon. member's party if not himself-I do not remember whether he was here or not- voted to make this discrimination much more violent, by voting for a motion to add another $125 million to that tax which would have tripled the present rate at least.
He went on at some length with regard to the fact that this whole resolution should be withdrawn, except for the tax relief given for certain drugs. I have listened to him. He wants the sales tax removed, the excise tax of 15 per cent removed, the excise tax of 25 per cent removed. He also wants the excise tax on cigarettes removed. In this house we have heard him urge much bigger personal income tax exemptions which, of course, would lessen our revenue. But I

have never heard him suggest that the corporation tax should be increased. I am confident that when we come to it, we shall also find that he is advocating a reduction in the corporation tax or perhaps the abolition of it. In other words, he is against every tax proposal we can make. I want to tell him just one thing. We are in this period of increased expenses because of our needs for defence; and defence costs money. It is not a torrent of words such as he has unleashed on us for the fourth time that will pay for our defence preparations. Those preparations need money, and this is the way the government of Canada has decided to raise the money required. These are the proposals which have been prepared to accomplish that purpose. No doubt the hon. member will give us the same speech he has just delivered when we have before us the excise tax bill, the income tax bill and the customs tariff bill. No doubt he will make part of the same speech when we get into the individual items of each of the bills. But inasmuch as he is so violently opposed to all these tax changes, I should like him somewhere, some place, to indicate where we can get this extra $400 million to pay for the increased defence costs we all support.

I do not like these commodity taxes in particular, and I am not altogether satisfied that there is not a feasible alternative in the capital gains tax. The minister dealt with that matter last Thursday evening, but I do not think he explained why that tax would not raise the necessary money we could get from these commodity taxes. It seems to me that a capital gains tax is a tax which would affect people who are making money through speculation-for instance, people who bought stocks a few years ago at $3 and $4 and who have sold them for from $50 to $75 to $100. It seems to me to be reasonable that they should have to pay some kind of a tax. It seems to me that about the only way in which any Canadian today can amass great wealth is by capital gains. I do not think any Canadian today can pay his taxes as he goes along and make a fortune, except through capital gains. I therefore respectfully suggest again that the minister or the parliamentary assistant might be well advised to tax this group of people rather than people who are starting out in life and who must buy these appliances.
One of the arguments that he will probably throw back at me in a minute is that if we tax capital gains we have to allow for losses: I do not see that that procedure necessarily would have to follow. If you had a
Excise Tax Act
modest tax on those capital gains, of say 10 per cent-and I admit that I do not know what revenue that would bring in-or 15 per cent, I do not see why losses have to come into it at all. If that argument does not make sense, I should be glad if the minister would tell me. But he does not have to be quite as sarcastic as he was with the hon. member for Eglinton a moment' or so ago.
The hon. member wants soft treatment.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. member's request for an expression of the government's attitude was couched in reasonable terms. He did not work himself into a passion. I shall therefore be glad to answer in the same reasonable way. The capital gains tax is of course now in use in the United States. Those administering it find it a very difficult tax to administer; they find it more difficult than the income tax. There is this point to be considered. Once you begin taxing capital gains, you must in turn allow a man to offset capital losses against capital gains. But I think the chief opposition to a capital gains tax in this country is the fact that here, where there is such a great need for development, especially in the pioneer parts of the country, we must give some incentive to the people to put their money into venture capital, in our mines, in our forests, in aluminum plants and things like that. As the hon. member pointed out, there is to be considered the rate of return which you can get back today, with the corporation tax and personal income tax as it is. There is the fact, for example, that the hon. member's leader has already spokem unfavourably on the fact that we are going: to permit public utilities to make five percent. Why should anybody venture capital: if that is the best they can ever expect from risking their capital in some new brave enterprise in northern Ontario, in northern: Quebec, in northern Saskatchewan oc ini British Columbia, when they can do better with no risk by putting that money in government bonds or in some safe established business? I think that in this country the fact that we have not had a capital gains tax has been one of the incentive factors which have been responsible-and I said one of the factors-for this large advent in Canada of United States capital which has been extremely helpful in building up this country/ in the post-war years.
But if the tax was 10 percent or 15 per cent, I do not think it would discourage that development about which the-parliamentary assistant speaks.

speechtext: The Americans felt that if the capital gains tax was to be worth while, it should be of the order of the tax they have, which is 25 per cent. If, as you say, some people venture boldly and in the end make considerable money as a reward-and for everyone who makes money, for example in the mines, as I know very well, there are a dozen who lose money- they create work and industry and associated development in this country; and if they make fortunes, we catch up with them eventually through succession duties.

For the benefit of the hon. member for Moose Jaw, it seems to me that it should be pointed out to him that there has -been a depreciation in the purchasing value of money. While I am on my feet, and getting back to this sales tax itself, I wonder if the government gave any consideration to keeping the sales tax at the same eight per cent rate and removing some of the exemptions which they now allow? My own experience with the application of these exemptions which are allowed with regard to certain goods that are put into manufacturing plants for use directly in the manufacture of goods is that it has become a regular menagerie, as I am quite sure the Minister of National Revenue very well knows. There is neither rhyme nor reason with regard to the way the exemptions are applied. I do not think even the minister is always convinced as to whether an exemption should or should not apply. I am wondering just how much revenue could have been derived by the government by the application of the eight per cent sales tax o all goods that are produced in Canada, thus getting away from the anomalies and inequities that are now in effect in the application of the act. For instance, with regard to a logging truck that is brought in and which it is conceded is used directly in the manufacture or production of logs, they will concede that the horn on there that goes "peep, peep" is not subject to sales tax. They will concede that is part of the truck. But if you go ahead and put a radio telephone on the truck in order to expedite and facilitate the use of the truck, in order to get more trips per day and in order to produce logs more cheaply, the authorities say no, that the radio telephone you instal is subject to sales

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, at times we seem to get so far from the primary purpose of this budget, which is to raise revenue to meet increased defence costs of the country and) to maintain the public services in this country which we provided long before Korea.

If that is the primary purpose of the budget, in the remarks which the parliamentary assistant made just a few moments ago in connection with logging machinery and so forth, he admitted that one of the purposes of the budget also was to take the tax off material used in industry, so that there would be no double taxes, in order to encourage industry. If there is any industry that should be encouraged it is the industry of education. This is one way in which we can encourage that industry. It is much more important to encourage it than to encourage the logging industry or any other industry. Once more I say that not only does the parliamentary assistant's answer fail to meet the argument, but it is not an answer.
The other matter that I brought up was in connection with gasoline trucks used exclusively in the production of coal. The only thing that the parliamentary assistant had to say about that was that diesel trucks used in this way are not subject to sales tax because they are big trucks, and they could not readily be used for any other purpose. Some of these gasoline-powered trucks used for that purpose are just as big as any of the diesel trucks, and I can really see no reason why the gasoline-powered truck should not be put in exactly the same position as the diesel truck. It is true that the diesel truck costs more money, but that is not a matter which should come into it. If we want to bring that argument into it, if the sales tax was put on the diesel truck the government would get more revenue out of it; but they have seen the reasonableness of taking the sales tax off those vehicles which are used exclusively in the production of coal, the purpose being to encourage the coal industry. There seems to be no reason whatever why the same course could not be followed with the gasoline-powered trucks as is followed with diesel trucks.

I want to say a few words in support of what I thought was a very reasonable and intelligent proposal made by the hon. member for Moose Jaw, namely, that there is a place in our taxation system for a capital gains tax. The parliamentary

assistant denies that, and says that to some extent it would discourage the people who want to invest venture capital. I can see some argument in that point of view, but many capital gains are made at the present time which are not the result of venture capital. For instance, what about sweepstakes, where a person may win a very large sum of money as a result of a sweepstake and pay no tax to this government on the winnings. The same applies to race track gambling.
Then there is another form of gambling. I have in mind particularly an instance in my own constituency of an American concern that has control over some thirty square miles of timber. During that whole period all they have paid is their timber limits tax to the provincial government. They prevented the development of the large area and refused to sell timber. At the same time local people who owned land had to pay taxes to build roads and schools and provide other facilities. This large American concern purchased the property for a song about forty-five years ago, and has arrested the development of a Canadian industry and a Canadian resource in that whole area. The result has been an increased price in lumber. Because of the great demand for lumber these people are in a position to sell timber contracts at five hundred times their original value. As a matter of fact they have been a blight on the Canadian economy ever since they became owners of the property.
I cannot see why people under those circumstances should not be required to pay capital gains tax to the government. And then I would mention one other point in connection with people who have purchased war assets. All of us know of people who have purchased war assets for a song from the government and are now able to resell those assets back to the government at an immense increase in price. Now, is that fixed capital doing anything to increase the production or improve the economy of the country? It is a straight gamble out of which they are reaping a great profit. I do suggest in all seriousness that here is a place where the capital gains tax should be applied so as to procure income, rather than to increase taxes on household necessities.

(3)	The wives and minor children of (2).
(d)	That the foregoing be without prejudice to the remaining taxation exemptions conferred by article XVII of the agreement.
Customs and Excise Exemptions
(a)	That the customs and excise exemptions accorded to contractor-owned equipment under the terms of article XIV (1) (a) of the leased bases agreement be suspended by an exchange of notes:
(b)	That it be agreed by exchange of notes that article XIV (1) (d) does not accord customs and/or excise exemptions in personal belongings and household effects of contractors and their U.S. employees (after first arrival) or customs and/or excise exemption on purchases in Canada, outside the leased areas, by U.S. military or civilian personnel, or their families:
(c)	That the U.S. authorities continue to exercise every precaution to prevent abuse of the customs and excise privileges enjoyed under the leased: bases agreement.
Post Offices
That it be agreed by exchange of notes that the U.S. military postal system in operation at the Newfoundland bases conform to the following stipulations:
(a)	That they provide military postal services only for U.S. military agencies, U.S. military personnel, authorized U.S. civilians, and their dependents,
(b)	That they dispatch mail only to the United States, its possessions and territories and its military postal installations,
(c)	That geographical locations be not indicated by date stamp or cancellation stamp.
Jurisdiction
(a)	That the government of the United States, through an exchange of diplomatic notes, agree to waive its rights of jurisdiction under the leased bases agreement over Canadian citizens, other British subjects, and alien civilians other than those subject to U.S. military law by reason of their accompanying or serving with the U.S. forces.
(b)	(1) That the governments of the United States and of Canada, through an exchange of diplomatic notes, agree to suspend the exercise of their rights of jurisdiction under article IV of the leased bases agreement other than those waived by the U.S. government under (a) above, for a period of five years, and thereafter subject to six months' notification of termination, except that in the event of war or other emergency the suspension shall, on notification given by either government, cease to operate;
(2) That the Canadian government, as a condition precedent to the waiver and suspension of the exercise of rights under article IV and to the extension to Newfoundland of an amended Visiting Forces (United States of America) Act, give satisfactory assurances that the U.S. officials in Newfoundland will have a degree of jurisdiction comparable to that which they now in fact exercise. In this connection, the U.S. section would regard the proposed letter from the government of Canada to the government of Newfoundland, with a reply from the Newfoundland government that jurisdictional conditions would remain substantially as now exercised, as the basis for satisfactory assurances to be given by the Canadian government.
(c)	That the Canadian government undertake to seek legislation to protect U.S. interests in security offences as envisaged by article V of the leased bases agreement.
(dj That the Canadian government seek amendment to the Visiting Forces (United States of America) Act to provide for the compulsory attendance of witnesses required by U.S. service courts.
(e)	That either government should be free to raise through appropriate channels the matter of any difficulties arising out of the working of the foregoing jurisdictional arrangements.
